A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEAL. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, and implementation listings, support a reliable comparison. Changed experimental conditions limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent comparison of the documents.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, including baseline comparisons, architectural ablations, plasticity measurements, and curriculum, reward, observability, and designated-role studies.

after.justification: v3 reports original experimental results throughout Section 5 and the appendices, including expanded baseline evaluations, long task sequences, partner adaptation, coordination analyses, and additional environments.

M1.justification: The core Overcooked generator and actor–critic architectures remain. v3 adds limited procedural extensions: Online MAS maintains running parameter-importance estimates, while Appendix L.1 introduces forced-coordination validation constraints and adapts the soup estimator to agents' combined reachable regions.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates Overcooked settings. v3 additionally evaluates JAXNAV, SMAX, and MPE SimpleSpread, spanning continuous navigation and heterogeneous combat tasks. It also adds adaptation to eight frozen partners across four hand-designed Overcooked layouts and scenarios with changing recipe requirements, cooking times, and movement dynamics.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Online MAS, ER-ACE, and PackNet and removes L2 from the main comparison. The architectural ablation substitutes ER-ACE for L2. v3 also evaluates HAPPO and expands MAPPO participation through the algorithm comparison in Figure 16 and the revised observability experiment.

E3.justification: The default training budget increases from 10^7 to 10^8 steps per task. Table 6 changes parallel environments from 16 to 2048, rollout length from 128 to 400, and several optimization settings. Forgetting measurement and experimental designs also change. Evaluation frequency changes from 100 to five updates in Table 6, although v3 Section 5 still states 100.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled 10-versus-100-task comparisons, neuron-dormancy analysis, comparisons across MARL algorithms, isolated and combined dynamics perturbations, forced-coordination tests, and measurements of role specialization and coordination forgetting. Observability analysis gains CNN controls. The earlier curriculum, reward, and designated-role studies remain present under reorganized appendices.

E5.justification: Both versions generally report five seeds and 95% confidence intervals. v3 Tables 4 and 9 additionally provide intervals for sequence-averaged plasticity summaries that v2 Table 4 presented as point estimates. This expands uncertainty reporting without establishing any increase in replication.

E6.justification: Table 2 substantially revises retained methods' results and rankings: v2's score leaders are EWC on Levels 1–2 and Online EWC on Level 3, whereas v3 reports PackNet leading all three. New results cover long sequences, partners, coordination, and additional environments. These are revised or newly reported outcomes under changed settings, rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 defines forgetting through differences between averaged post-training and final scores. v3 replaces this with nonnegative fractional performance drops aggregated over time using exponential weights, changing the mathematical quantity substantially. Appendix L.3 additionally defines a Jensen–Shannon-based heterogeneity index and coordination forgetting.

C1.justification: The introduction expands the benchmark contribution from procedurally generated Overcooked tasks to four cooperative environments. The abstract and conclusion foreground the new claim that long sequences reveal failures and alter experimental conclusions. v3 also elevates changing partners and the distinction between coordination retention and performance retention within its central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations of long-sequence over-regularization, coordination changes beneath stable scores, and method-dependent benefits of separate partner heads. The observability discussion shifts from centralized-critic interference toward interactions between observability and encoder choice. Limitations acknowledge partner and dynamics variation while emphasizing restricted recipe semantics and task-incremental evaluation.

D1.justification: v3 expands documentation with update and gradient-step accounting, partner-population training parameters and ordering, perturbation ranges, and task-generation details for additional environments. Hardware and timing disclosures change from A100 to H100 experiments. The GitHub access link and original MLP/CNN specifications remain, while the conflicting evaluation frequencies reduce reproducibility clarity.

R1.justification: Related work gains substantive positioning against Lifelong Hanabi, RPG, COMAD, and additional accelerated benchmarking platforms. It expands discussion of constructing continual benchmarks from existing simulators and distinguishes MEAL through scalable, hardware-accelerated continual evaluation. These changes extend research positioning substantially beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting around long-sequence evaluation. Environment specifications, reward analysis, and limitations move into appendices, and the appendix organization expands around coordination, partners, and additional domains. This substantially changes the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column layout. Baseline confidence intervals move into the main results table from separate appendix tables, and ablation and observability displays are redesigned. New displays include long-sequence plots, an algorithm-comparison heatmap, partner-adaptation panels, coordination tables, and illustrations of additional environments.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v2 through actual 100-task comparisons, partner adaptation, and evaluation beyond Overcooked. However, new reporting inconsistencies limit confidence: Section 5 and Table 6 disagree on evaluation frequency, and Table 15 reports SMAX forgetting of 1.33–1.71 without explaining how this accords with Equations 2–3, which bound forgetting by one for nonnegative scores and positive reference scores. These issues affect reproducibility and interpretation of the expanded evidence, leaving the net quality improvement uncertain.
